section_summary: This section opens with cross-reference sheets and consular reports on alien-employment restrictions, the admission of foreign entertainers, and Korean labor migration into Japan. Later documents trace labor developments from 1935 through 1940, including unemployment, wages and working hours, seamen’s and arsenal workers’ unions, strikes, military interference in organized labor, and increasingly comprehensive wartime labor controls. Emigration to Korea and Manchuria, industrial mobilization, and the proposed dissolution of trade unions are recurring themes.

subfiles.title: Document File Note: Alien Employment Restrictions in Japan
subfiles.about: The card cross-references a Tokyo despatch transmitting a report on restrictions affecting alien employment in Japan.
subfiles.summary: This filing note identifies Despatch No. 114 from Hutchinson in Tokyo concerning alien-employment restrictions. It states that a copy of the underlying report was attached and points to file 800.504/36.

subfiles.title: Document File Note: Korean Laborers and the Labor Situation in Japan
subfiles.about: The card references a detailed report asserting that Korean laborers were becoming a threat to Japanese labor.
subfiles.summary: The filing note describes a June 1934 report on the Japanese labor situation. Its central concern is the growing presence of Korean laborers and their perceived effect on Japanese workers.

subfiles.title: Document File Note: Strike at the Osaka Mechanical Works
subfiles.about: The card references Despatch No. 917 concerning a strike at the Osaka Mechanical Works.
subfiles.summary: This note identifies an Embassy report on a major strike at the Osaka Mechanical Works. It cross-references the report to the political-report file 894.00 P.R./80.

subfiles.title: Labor and Emigration: Osaka Strike and Population Policy
subfiles.about: The excerpt discusses the Osaka Mechanical Works strike, proposed compulsory intervention in labor disputes, and Japanese views on emigration as a remedy for population pressure.
subfiles.summary: More than one thousand Osaka Mechanical Works employees struck after wage and concession demands were rejected, while patriotic leagues pressed for settlement because the plant held Army and Navy orders. The report also notes a contemplated Home Affairs bill for compulsory government intervention in damaging labor disputes. At a student conference in Tokyo, Japanese delegates rejected birth control as impractical and proposed emigration to Korea, with Koreans moving onward to Manchukuo.

subfiles.title: Document File Note: Report No. 145 on Foreign Entertainers
subfiles.about: The card introduces a detailed report on the temporary admission and residence of foreign musicians, actors, artists, and choristers in Japan.
subfiles.summary: The note identifies Report No. 145 as a response concerning Japanese rules for foreign entertainers. It highlights the Kaili troupe, Hawaiian Americans who were expelled after authorities found their employment arrangements insufficient.

subfiles.title: Report No. 145: Conditions of Temporary Admission and Residence of Musicians, Actors, Artists, and Choristers
subfiles.from: J. M. Allison, American Vice Consul; approved by Arthur Garrels, American Consul General
subfiles.about: The report explains Japanese immigration rules and police practices governing foreign entertainers, using the Kaili troupe's expulsion as a case study.
subfiles.summary: Japan had no special statute for musicians, actors, artists, or choristers, but admitted them under general nonimmigrant regulations and subjected them to unusually strict police scrutiny. Entertainers commonly needed guarantees from responsible Japanese organizations, and transit-visa holders could be required to leave after thirty days. The experience of Mr. and Mrs. Kaili and Pearl Kama illustrates the arbitrary application of these rules: despite valid visas, employment contracts, and willing guarantors, the troupe was ordered out of Japan. The report concludes that inconsistent and sometimes unreasonable police administration caused substantial foreign dissatisfaction.

subfiles.title: Document File Note: Report No. 146 on Other Alien Employees
subfiles.about: The card introduces a report on temporary admission and residence for alien workers other than entertainers.
subfiles.summary: This filing note identifies Report No. 146 as a companion to Report No. 145. It states that the report addresses foreign employees who were not musicians, actors, artists, or choristers and responds to the Department's September 14 instruction.

subfiles.title: Report No. 146: Temporary Admission and Residence of Other Aliens for Employment
subfiles.from: J. M. Allison, American Vice Consul; approved by Arthur Garrels, American Consul General
subfiles.about: The report states that Japan had no special rules for temporary alien employees beyond the general regulations described in earlier reports.
subfiles.summary: Allison reports that no special Japanese regulations covered foreign employees outside the entertainment categories addressed in Report No. 145. He refers the Department to Hutchinson's November 1932 study of alien-employment restrictions and states that the governing regulations had not changed.

subfiles.title: Document File Note: Nagoya Industrial and Labor Conditions
subfiles.about: The note records the transmission of five copies of a pamphlet on Nagoya's industrial and labor conditions.
subfiles.summary: The Nagoya consulate forwarded five copies of a pamphlet published by the Nagoya Chamber of Commerce and Industry. The pamphlet itself is not reproduced in this section.

subfiles.title: Document File Note: Report No. 148 on Korean Labor Migration
subfiles.about: The card introduces a report on Japanese efforts to limit Korean labor migration without openly discriminating against colonial subjects.
subfiles.summary: The filing note identifies Report No. 148 on the labor situation in Japan. It emphasizes the authorities' dilemma of discouraging Korean laborers while avoiding charges of discrimination or unfair treatment of colonials.

subfiles.title: Report No. 148: Korean Immigration and the Trend of Migratory Movements
subfiles.from: J. M. Allison, American Vice Consul; approved by Arthur Garrels, American Consul General
subfiles.about: The report supplements an earlier study with Japanese Home Ministry statistics and analysis of Korean immigration into Japan proper.
subfiles.summary: Allison supplements Report No. 143 with Home Ministry figures on Korean migration and encloses a translation of the ministry's findings. He observes that the annual increase in Japan's Korean population rose sharply between the earlier period and 1929–1933. Skilled as well as unskilled Koreans were entering the labor force, and Japanese officials sought ways to reduce the influx without appearing to discriminate against colonial subjects.

subfiles.title: Enclosure: Korean Immigrants in Japan
subfiles.about: The translated enclosure describes the scale, labor effects, and welfare problems associated with Korean migration to Japan proper.
subfiles.summary: The report gives annual estimates of the Korean population in Japan from 1929 through 1933 and describes increases of roughly 20,000 to 80,000 people a year. It argues that low-paid Korean workers increasingly displaced Japanese laborers in both unskilled and skilled employment during the depression. Because Koreans were treated legally as Japanese subjects after annexation, the government rejected formal immigration restrictions while urging indigent prospective migrants to reconsider leaving Korea. That protective policy was reportedly misunderstood in Korea as an attempt to restrict migration.

subfiles.title: Document File Note: Japanese Unemployment in March 1935
subfiles.about: The note references an unofficial Home Office report comparing unemployment in March 1935 with March 1934.
subfiles.summary: This filing card identifies Despatch No. 1427 on Japanese unemployment. It records that the figures came from a Home Office report issued on July 16.

subfiles.title: Labor and Migration: Unemployment in Japan
subfiles.about: The excerpt reports a year-over-year decline in the number of unemployed Japanese workers.
subfiles.summary: A Home Office report placed unemployment in Japan at 367,542 on March 1, 1935. This represented a decrease of 17,801 from March 1, 1934; the information was obtained through the Commercial Attaché.

subfiles.title: Document File Note: Labor Laws and Nissan Jidosha Employment
subfiles.about: The note reports that labor-law obligations allegedly compelled Nissan Jidosha to retain workers and manufacture Datsun automobiles faster than they could be sold.
subfiles.summary: This Yokohama filing note concerns the effect of Japanese labor law on automobile production. It says Nissan Jidosha continued overproducing Datsun automobiles because it was required to keep its existing workforce employed.

subfiles.title: Document File Note: Imperial Ordinances Governing Alien Residence
subfiles.about: The note introduces translations of two 1899 imperial ordinances affecting the permanent residence of aliens in Japan.
subfiles.summary: The filing note describes Imperial Ordinances Nos. 352 and 421 of July 28, 1899. Although designed chiefly to permit the residence of aliens other than laborers, the ordinances also affected the permanent entry of foreign farmers, fishermen, miners, and related workers.

subfiles.title: Document File Note: Discharge Allowance Law and Tokyo Elections
subfiles.about: The note references the new Discharge Allowance Law and the Social Mass Party's gains in the Tokyo Prefectural Assembly.
subfiles.summary: This card identifies Despatch No. 1942 on labor benefits and electoral developments. It notes that the Discharge Allowance Law would take effect on January 1, 1937, and that the Social Mass Party had won twenty-two Tokyo assembly seats.

subfiles.title: Labor and Emigration: Discharge Allowances and the Social Mass Party
subfiles.about: The excerpt quantifies coverage under the Discharge Allowance Law and records Social Mass Party electoral gains in Tokyo.
subfiles.summary: The report states that 1,335,736 workers in 6,175 industrial plants would benefit from the Discharge Allowance Law beginning January 1, 1937. It also reports that the Social Mass Party won twenty-two seats in the June 10 Tokyo Prefectural Assembly election, compared with one seat previously.

subfiles.title: Document File Note: Labor and Emigration Developments of July 1936
subfiles.about: The card references a report on Japanese labor and emigration developments during July 1936.
subfiles.summary: This filing note identifies Despatch No. 1991 as a monthly report on labor and emigration. The attached excerpt addresses Socialist politics, a threatened seamen's strike, and large-scale settlement in Manchuria.

subfiles.title: Labor and Emigration: Social Mass Party, Seamen, and Manchurian Settlement
subfiles.about: The report covers Social Mass Party policy, averted seamen's industrial action, and a proposed program for settling Japanese emigrants in Manchuria.
subfiles.summary: At its July 16 Osaka meeting, the Social Mass Party endorsed parliamentary government for workers, nationalization of major industries, economic stabilization, and the overthrow of the Hirota Cabinet. A threatened New Japan Seamen's Union strike was avoided after shipowners recognized collective-bargaining rights. The Overseas Ministry reportedly planned to settle five million Japanese in Manchuria over twelve years, beginning with 50,000 emigrants in fiscal year 1937–1938.

subfiles.title: Document File Note: Proposed State Control of Labor
subfiles.about: The note references measures being prepared for state control of labor resembling Nazi labor legislation.
subfiles.summary: This card identifies Despatch No. 2046 on proposed Japanese labor-control measures. It characterizes the planned system as similar to Nazi state control of labor.

subfiles.title: Labor-Control Bill and Social Mass Party Opposition
subfiles.about: The excerpt describes the paternalist principles of a labor-control bill and the Social Mass Party's attack on defense spending and the Hirota Cabinet.
subfiles.summary: The Home Office presented capital and labor as bound by reciprocal duties to society and the state, with government acting as an impartial mediator. The Social Mass Party opposed higher defense expenditure, renewed its no-confidence position toward the Hirota Cabinet, and warned that government policy would increase the burdens on workers.

subfiles.title: Document File Note: Labor Questions and the Army
subfiles.about: The note references a discussion of current labor questions, particularly their connection with the Japanese Army.
subfiles.summary: This filing card identifies Despatch No. 2048 on labor and the Army. It points to file 894.00/672 for the original paper.

subfiles.title: G-2 Report No. 8464: Government Relations with Labor
subfiles.about: The report analyzes an Army order forcing arsenal workers to leave labor unions and the political, union, and press reaction to it.
subfiles.summary: The War Office ordered civilian employees at military arsenals, including workers at Nagoya and Kokura, to sever union affiliations and pledge not to join new unions. Labor federations and the Social Mass Party protested the coercive methods, while Kanju Kato's anti-Army faction demanded resistance and a popular front; even pro-Army leaders Hisashi Aso and Kan'ichiro Kamei objected. General Yamawaki denied that the measure foreshadowed militarization of private industry, but the Home Office and press feared precisely that consequence. The report concludes that the controversy revealed growing resistance to Army intrusions on civil liberties and organized labor.

subfiles.title: Document File Note: International Labor Conference and Seamen's Strikes
subfiles.about: The note references Japan's position on international labor standards and seamen's strikes during February 1937.
subfiles.summary: This card identifies Despatch No. 2314 on the forthcoming International Labor Conference in Geneva. It also flags disputes involving the forty-hour week, minimum working age, and seamen's unions.

subfiles.title: Labor: International Standards and February 1937 Seamen's Strikes
subfiles.about: The report covers Japanese opposition to international working-time standards and two very different seamen's labor disputes.
subfiles.summary: Japan's delegation was expected to oppose the forty-hour week at Geneva, while Japanese employers opposed raising the minimum age for factory work. Crews of the Tosa Steamship Company struck after being pressed to leave the Japan Seamen's Union and demanded minimum wages, retirement allowances, and regular raises; managing director Tamikichi Kobayashi committed suicide amid the conflict. The Meirokai separately struck against Nippon Yusen Kaisha, accusing it of lèse-majesté for failing to fly flags during an Osaka naval review.

subfiles.title: Document File Note: Settlement of the Meirokai Strike
subfiles.about: The card references settlement of the Meirokai strike and Army conditions for merging the new and old seamen's unions.
subfiles.summary: This filing note identifies Despatch No. 2368 on the February 28 Meirokai strike against Nippon Yusen Kaisha. It also notes two Army demands concerning the proposed consolidation of Japanese seamen's organizations.

subfiles.title: Labor: Meirokai Settlement and Army Conditions for Seamen's Union Merger
subfiles.about: The excerpt reports the settlement of the flag controversy and Army pressure on the proposed unified seamen's union.
subfiles.summary: The Meirokai strike ended March 15 after Nippon Yusen Kaisha admitted fault for not flying flags and the union apologized for the inconvenience caused. The Osaka gendarmerie reportedly required a unified seamen's union to break with social-democratic organizations and dismiss Japan Seamen's Union vice president Manryo Yonekubo because of his criticism of the Manchurian Incident.

subfiles.title: Document File Note: Labor Situation in April 1937
subfiles.about: The note references proposed working-hour restrictions, suppression of May Day demonstrations, and wage unrest.
subfiles.summary: This card identifies Despatch No. 2422 on the April 1937 labor situation. It highlights a working-hours bill, a ban on May Day parades, and agitation over wages.

subfiles.title: Labor: Working-Hour Bill, May Day Ban, and Wage Increases
subfiles.about: The excerpt describes a proposed twelve-hour limit, restrictions on May Day activity, and wage settlements prompted by rising living costs.
subfiles.summary: The Home Ministry was preparing legislation to limit work uniformly to twelve hours a day in the interest of national health. It also banned union parades and demonstrations on May Day. Rising living costs produced substantial unrest, with settlements or voluntary company actions raising wages by approximately 8 to 15 percent.

subfiles.title: Labor Disputes and the Kobe Streetcar Strike
subfiles.doc_type: document file note with report excerpt
subfiles.about: The document reports a sharp increase in labor disputes and the termination of a Kobe municipal streetcar strike amid the North China crisis.
subfiles.summary: A Home Office survey counted 1,332 disputes involving 169,797 people during the first five months of 1937, nearly twice as many disputes and five times as many participants as in the comparable 1936 period. About five hundred Kobe municipal streetcar employees struck for higher wages on July 6. They returned on July 19 after Hyogo authorities invoked the North China situation, although one newspaper described the decision as voluntary.

subfiles.title: Document File Note: Wartime Abolition of Strikes
subfiles.about: The card references an All-Japan Federation of Labor resolution calling for an end to strikes during the Sino-Japanese conflict.
subfiles.summary: This filing note identifies Despatch No. 2654 on wartime labor policy. It highlights the labor federation's October 17 resolution to abolish strikes throughout industry during the conflict with China.

subfiles.title: Labor: All-Japan Federation's Wartime Program
subfiles.about: The excerpt sets out a wartime no-strike policy and reports a Japanese seamen's protest against American labor organizations.
subfiles.summary: The All-Japan Federation of Labor urged peaceful settlement of disputes, abolition of strikes, a tripartite committee to prevent profiteering, and national control of industry and labor during the China conflict. The Japanese Seamen's Union in Kobe also protested to the American Federation of Labor and the Committee for Industrial Organization after those bodies denounced Japan as an aggressor in China.

subfiles.title: Document File Note: Raw-Material Controls, Unemployment, and Munitions Labor
subfiles.about: The card references anticipated unemployment from raw-material restrictions and measures to secure skilled labor for munitions.
subfiles.summary: This filing note identifies Despatch No. 3094 on the labor effects of government material controls. It contrasts optimistic official plans for absorbing or assisting the unemployed with new controls over skilled munitions workers.

subfiles.title: Labor: Projected Unemployment and Compulsory Registration of Skilled Workers
subfiles.about: The excerpt forecasts mass unemployment from material restrictions and describes compulsory labor controls for munitions industries.
subfiles.summary: Finance and Welfare officials estimated that restrictions on thirty-two raw materials could leave 700,000 to 800,000 people unemployed, far above the 1931 peak. They expected war industries to absorb about half and believed relief could be provided for the remainder. The Cabinet also approved compulsory registration and licensed employment of technicians and skilled workers in munitions and allied industries.

subfiles.title: Cross-Reference File Note: Government Labor Measures in February 1940
subfiles.about: The sheet cross-references Despatch No. 4611 on the Japanese government's attitude toward labor and its February 1940 measures.
subfiles.summary: The cross-reference directs readers to political-report file 894.00 P.R./147 for the original paper. The referenced material concerns government labor policy and new controls adopted or announced in February 1940.

subfiles.title: Labor: Worker Diversion, Mobilization, and Expected Union Dissolution
subfiles.about: The report describes compulsory diversion of workers to urgent industries, planned labor mobilization, expected union dissolution, and declining productivity.
subfiles.summary: An ordinance under the National General Mobilization Law authorized the diversion of regulated groups of male and female workers to urgent industries and required nonessential producers to reduce staffing to 70 percent of their December 1939 levels. The government was preparing a broader labor-mobilization plan and expected labor unions to dissolve because they conflicted with the idea of industrial service to the state. Diet discussion attributed falling labor efficiency to low wages, rising living costs, employment restrictions, and long working hours.
